corruption_summary: Feminist liturgy corrupts the “Our Father” address by substituting gender-neutral or maternal language — denying that “Father” is the name revealed by Christ and not merely a cultural metaphor; Open Theism strips the Father-address of its covenantal security by denying the Father's exhaustive foreknowledge.
corruption_paragraphs: The feminist liturgical project — represented by Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, Sallie McFague (Models of God, 1987), and the Inclusive Language Lectionary tradition — treats “Our Father” as a patriarchal cultural projection onto deity rather than the name revealed by the Son. McFague proposed “Mother,” “Lover,” and “Friend” as equally valid models for God, dissolving the revealed name into a preference menu. This fails on the most basic point: Jesus did not teach His disciples to address God by a culturally appropriate metaphor of their choosing; He taught them to address God by the name the Son revealed. The Father-Son relation is not a figure of speech; it is the inner-Trinitarian ground of all prayer.

Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Greg Boyd, John Sanders) undermines the “Our Father” address from the other direction: if the Father does not possess exhaustive foreknowledge of the future, the creature's prayer becomes a collaboration of equals attempting to navigate an open future rather than a child approaching an omniscient, all-wise, sovereign Father who “knows what you need before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:8). The Lord's Prayer presupposes a Father who knows, governs, and can grant; Open Theism gives the child an uncertain colleague rather than an omnipotent Father.
roots_summary: The “Our Father” address flows from the Son's unique knowledge of the Father (Matthew 11:27), through the Spirit of adoption (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:15), and is grounded in the eternal Trinitarian relation that the Son's incarnation reveals to and applies for the elect.
roots_lines: Old Testament preparations (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8) — Israel's covenantal-national fatherhood language prepares the category without establishing the adoptive intimacy; these texts call God Father in the sense of Creator and covenant head, not the intimate access Christ opens.

Matthew 11:27 (exclusive knowledge) — the Son's unique and mutual knowledge of the Father is the theological ground for the disciples' address; only those to whom the Son reveals the Father can pray “Our Father.”

Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 (Spirit of adoption) — the Spirit who cries “Abba, Father” in the believer's heart is the same Spirit of the Son; the adopted children share the Son's prayer vocabulary because they share the Son's Spirit.

High-priestly prayer (John 17) — Jesus' own address to the Father in John 17 models the intimate, confident, covenant-grounded approach He teaches the disciples; “Holy Father” and “righteous Father” nuance the address with holiness and justice.

Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 100 — “The preface of the Lord's Prayer teacheth us to draw near to God with all holy reverence and confidence, as children to a father, able and ready to help us”; the catechism distills the adoptive confidence the address is designed to instill.
usage: To say “Our Father” with understanding is to make a Trinitarian claim: the Father addressed is the First Person of the Trinity, known only through the Son, approached only by the Spirit of adoption; every genuine prayer to the Father is therefore Trinitarian prayer, whether or not the structure is explicit.

The communal “our” rebukes private-religion Christianity: Christians do not have a personal Father distinct from the church's Father; to pray “Our Father” is to include the whole covenant family in the approach and to refuse the individualism that treats prayer as a private transaction.

The progressive feminist project to replace “Father” in the Lord's Prayer reveals its deepest assumption: that the Creator's revealed name is negotiable. Jesus taught one specific address — the name the Son gives to the one He knows by nature; to change it is to claim the authority to rename the God who has already named Himself.

pos: n. phrase (from Matthew 6:19–21; the eschatological wealth accumulated through single-hearted devotion to God rather than earthly accumulation)
etymology: Treasure from Old French tresor, Latin thesaurus, Greek thēsauros (storehouse, treasure). Heaven from Old English heofon (the sky, the dwelling of God). The phrase “treasure in heaven” appears in Matthew 6:20 and its parallel in Luke 12:33, and in the Rich Young Ruler pericope (Matthew 19:21; Mark 10:21; Luke 18:22). In each case Jesus identifies a form of eschatological wealth — permanent, imperishable, and located in God's domain — that stands in contrast to the perishable, stealable wealth accumulated on earth.
biblical_def: The command to “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:20) is the positive counterpart to the prohibition against laying up earthly treasures — where moth, rust, and thieves reduce everything to nothing. Jesus identifies the heart as the index of where one's real treasure is: “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (6:21). The movement of desire reveals the movement of the soul; treasure-location diagnoses heart-location. The Rich Young Ruler passage (Matthew 19:21) makes the application concrete: “If you wish to be complete, go and sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” The exchange is not abolition of wealth-aspiration but relocation of it from the perishable to the permanent. The immediately following verse in the Sermon (6:22–24) develops the diagnosis: the eye that is “single” (or “clear”) toward God allows the whole body to be full of light; the divided eye, attempting to serve both God and mammon, produces inner darkness. Treasure-in-heaven theology is thus a doctrine of single-heartedness before God — the undivided devotion that Augustine called the ordering of loves (ordo amoris): God is the supreme good toward whom all other goods are rightly ordered. The Puritan tradition (particularly Richard Baxter's Saints' Everlasting Rest) developed this into a full program of heavenly-mindedness: the Christian invests mental and emotional energy in the contemplation of eternal goods, so that earthly goods are properly relativized rather than despised.
webster_summary: Treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20) names the eschatological wealth accumulated through single-hearted devotion to God — permanent, imperishable goods that thieves cannot steal and moth cannot consume — contrasted with earthly accumulation as the true object of Christian desire.
webster_full: TREASURE IN HEAVEN, n. [Greek thēsauros en ouranō.] The eschatological wealth commanded by Christ in Matthew 6:20 as the object of Christian accumulation: imperishable goods located in God's domain, immune to moth, rust, and thieves, and permanently accessible. Contrasted with earthly treasures which are perishable, stealable, and corruptible.

Matthew 6:21 provides the heart-diagnostic: “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” The location of one's treasure reveals the location of one's heart. This makes treasure-in-heaven not merely a financial principle but a spiritual anthropology: the soul goes where it deposits its desires; heavenly treasure-deposit produces heavenly heart-orientation.

The “single eye” of Matthew 6:22–23 develops the same idea through the body's light-organ: an undivided eye directed toward God fills the whole body with light; a divided eye — trying to see both God and mammon simultaneously — produces inner darkness. Single-heartedness toward God is the condition of spiritual perception.

The Rich Young Ruler passage (Matthew 19:21) applies the principle pastorally: the ruler's treasure was his earthly wealth, and he could not relocate it to heaven at Christ's command. His departure “grieving” reveals that his heart had followed his treasure to earth; Jesus' command was not arbitrary poverty-advocacy but a diagnostic test of the heart's actual location.

Richard Baxter's The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) is the fullest Puritan development of the treasure-in-heaven doctrine: Baxter devotes the second half to “heavenly contemplation,” the practice of deliberately directing the mind toward eternal goods so that the affections are properly ordered. This is not world-denial but the reordering of loves: earthly goods are held lightly because better goods are held firmly.
scriptures: Matthew 6:19
Do not lay up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.
Matthew 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.
Matthew 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Matthew 6:24
No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel inverts the treasure-in-heaven command by promising earthly wealth as the evidence of heavenly favor; therapeutic evangelicalism reduces it to a life-balance principle; both suppress the radical single-heartedness and eschatological reorientation the command demands.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-gospel tradition — Kenneth Hagin, Creflo Dollar, Joel Osteen — inverts the treasure-in-heaven command by reading it as a principle for earthly enrichment: give to God now and receive back multiplied earthly wealth as proof of divine favor. This turns the eschatological reorientation Jesus commands into a this-age investment strategy with divine returns. Jesus' prohibition on earthly treasure-accumulation becomes a financial vehicle for the very accumulation He prohibited. The gospel's “exceeding great and precious promises” (2 Peter 1:4) are eschatological promises, not stock-market guarantees; and the Rich Young Ruler demonstrates that Jesus does not promise earthly wealth to those who divest for Him but treasure in the age to come.

A subtler corruption in evangelical culture reduces treasure-in-heaven to a life-balance principle: don't make money your everything, hold it loosely, maintain perspective. This retains the surface counsel while defusing the radical command. Jesus does not say “hold earthly treasure lightly” as a balance correction; He says “do not lay it up” and commands its active relocation. The Puritan heavenly-mindedness tradition (Baxter, Sibbes) understood that treasure-in-heaven requires not merely loosened grip on earthly goods but active, deliberate investment of desire in eternal goods — a positive practice of contemplating and longing for heaven, not merely tolerating earth.
roots_summary: The treasure-in-heaven teaching flows from Old Testament Wisdom's deprecation of perishable wealth (Proverbs 11:28; 23:4–5), the Psalter's orientation toward the LORD as the soul's true portion (Psalm 73:25–26), and the eschatological inheritance promised to the new-covenant community.
roots_lines: Proverbs 11:28 and 23:4–5 — “He who trusts in his riches will fall”; “Do not weary yourself to gain wealth”; the Wisdom tradition's persistent deprecation of earthly wealth as a final good prepares the soil for Jesus' command to relocate treasure to an imperishable domain.

Psalm 73:25–26 (God as portion) — “Whom have I in heaven but You? And besides You, I desire nothing on earth.” Asaph's confession of God as the soul's all-sufficient portion is the experiential equivalent of treasure-in-heaven: the heart that has found its treasure in God has stopped competing with earthly treasures.

Matthew 13:44 (treasure hidden in a field) — the man who finds the kingdom of heaven sells everything he has to buy the field; the parable enacts what the command prescribes — total reorientation of treasure-desire toward the one thing of supreme value.

Luke 12:33–34 (parallel command) — “Sell your possessions and give to charity; make yourselves purses which do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in heaven”; Luke's version ties the positive command to concrete act of generous giving as the mechanism of heavenly treasure-accumulation.

Richard Baxter, The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) — the most sustained Puritan development of heavenly-mindedness: Baxter prescribes a daily practice of “heavenly contemplation” to keep eternal goods vivid and earthly goods in their proper subordinate place.
usage: The heart-diagnostic of Matthew 6:21 (“where your treasure is, there will your heart be also”) is the most searching test of true conversion: not what one professes but where one's desires go when unguarded reveals the heart's actual treasure-location.

The Rich Young Ruler passage shows that the treasure-in-heaven command functions as a diagnostic test: Jesus did not give the same command to every petitioner (Zacchaeus was not told to sell everything), but He used it where the earthly treasure was the specific idol blocking the heart's access to the kingdom.

Puritan heavenly-mindedness (Baxter, Sibbes) is the practical discipline Jesus' command generates: not passive detachment from earthly goods but active cultivation of desire for heavenly ones — the soul must be trained to find God more satisfying than what replaces Him.

pos: adj./n. (from Old English wyrgan; anxious, distracted care about temporal things that displaces trust in God's sovereign provision)
etymology: From Old English wyrgan (to strangle, choke; said of a dog killing its prey by strangling), from Proto-Germanic *wurgjan. The image is visceral — worry as a strangling force that cuts off breath and peace. By extension the word came to mean anxious, consuming preoccupation. The Greek merimna / merimnao (used in Matthew 6:25–34) carries the sense of a divided, distracted mind — meros (part, division) + nous (mind): the worried person is the person whose mind has been split from its proper resting place in God.
biblical_def: Worry in the biblical account is not merely emotional discomfort but a theological disorder: the displacement of faith in God's sovereign provision by preoccupation with temporal contingencies. Jesus addresses it directly in Matthew 6:25–34, commanding “do not be anxious” (mē merimnate) three times and grounding the prohibition in the Father's care for His creation: the birds of the air are fed without sowing or reaping; the lilies of the field are clothed without labor — how much more will the heavenly Father provide for those He has made in His image? The argument is from the lesser to the greater: if God superintends His non-covenant creatures with providential care, His covenant children are infinitely more secure. Jesus identifies worry as the characteristic disposition of “the Gentiles” (Matthew 6:32) — those who have no covenant God and must scramble for themselves — and contrasts it with the kingdom-seeking that should govern the disciple: “But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (6:33). Philippians 4:6 provides the positive command alongside the prohibition: “Be anxious for nothing — but in everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” The antidote to worry is not stoic self-control but specific, thankful prayer that returns the burden to the sovereign God who governs all things. Worry is thus the practical evidence of failing to trust the God who knows what His children need before they ask (Matthew 6:8).
webster_summary: Worry (Greek merimna, divided mind) is the theological disorder of anxious, consuming preoccupation with temporal contingencies — the displacement of faith in God's sovereign provision by practical unbelief; forbidden by Christ in Matthew 6:25–34 and replaced by prayer and kingdom-seeking.
webster_full: WORRY, v./n. [Old English wyrgan, to strangle.] To afflict with distressing uneasiness; to be anxious or solicitous about temporal contingencies. The root image is of being strangled — worry as a force that cuts off the ease and peace that trust in God should produce. In biblical usage, the Greek merimna (from meros, part; divided) names the anxious, distracted mind that has lost its resting place in God.

Jesus' threefold prohibition in Matthew 6:25–34 (“do not be anxious”) treats worry not as a personality type but as a sin — specifically the sin of practical unbelief in the Father's sovereign and attentive provision. The prohibition is commanded, not merely advised; its violation is addressed as a failure of faith, not a natural emotional limitation.

The two analogies (birds fed, lilies clothed, Matt. 6:26–30) employ the a fortiori argument: if God provides for non-covenant creatures that neither labor nor store, His covenant children under His particular care are infinitely more securely provided for. The argument is not “relax; things usually work out” but “the sovereign Father who sustains all creation governs your life; distrust of His governance is the root of your worry.”

The identification of worry with “the Gentiles” (Matthew 6:32) is theologically precise: those without covenant access to the God who knows and provides are correctly anxious by rational necessity. The Christian who worries is acting like one who has no Father — living as if the covenant were not real, as if prayer were ineffective, as if God did not know what His children needed.

Philippians 4:6–7 completes the biblical picture: “Be anxious for nothing — but in everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” The antidote is specific prayer, not general trust; the result is divine peace that cannot be manufactured by willpower but is given by the God to whom the worried soul has entrusted its burden.
scriptures: Matthew 6:25

For this reason I say to you, do not be anxious for your life, as to what you shall eat, or what you shall drink — nor for your body, as to what you shall put on. Is not life more than food, and the body than clothing?
Matthew 6:33
But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness — and all these things shall be added to you.
Matthew 6:34
Therefore do not be anxious for tomorrow. For tomorrow will care for itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.
Philippians 4:6
Be anxious for nothing — but in everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic culture has reclassified worry as a medical condition (anxiety disorder) requiring pharmacological and psychological intervention rather than a theological disorder requiring repentance, prayer, and renewed trust in God's sovereign provision; while prosperity theology promises that obedient believers need never face the occasions of worry.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern psychology and psychiatry have reclassified worry-as-sin as anxiety-as-disorder, treating anxious preoccupation primarily as a neurological or environmental condition to be managed through medication, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and therapeutic self-work. This framework is not entirely wrong — genuine anxiety disorders with neurological components are real and deserve compassionate care — but it cannot remain the primary register for the pastor, because the New Testament treats ordinary worry as a theological failure, not a medical one. Jesus does not say “manage your anxiety through evidence-based techniques”; He says “do not be anxious” and grounds the command in the Father's covenant faithfulness. The therapeutic reclassification systematically replaces the call to faith with the call to technique.

Prosperity-gospel theology creates the opposite error: it promises that the truly believing, tithing, confessing Christian will be exempt from the circumstances that generate worry — guaranteed health, financial provision, and favorable outcomes. This eliminates the occasion of the Philippians 4:6 command by promising that obedient believers will not face situations that tempt to worry. Jesus, however, located His prohibition in the context of ordinary earthly life — food, drink, clothing, tomorrow — not in a circumstantially protected existence. The peace of God (Phil. 4:7) is promised to those who pray under pressure, not to those who have been shielded from pressure by divine favor.
roots_summary: The biblical treatment of worry flows from the Psalter's cast-your-burden tradition (Psalm 55:22; 37:5), the Mosaic covenant's promise of divine provision (Deuteronomy 8:3), and the prophets' “fear not” commands to Israel in covenant relationship with the providing God.
roots_lines: Deuteronomy 8:3 (manna theology) — God fed Israel with manna to teach them that “man shall not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God”; the manna lesson is the Old Testament version of Matthew 6:25 — earthly provision comes from the word of God, not human industry alone.

Psalm 55:22 (casting the burden) — “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you”; the Psalter's consistent direction of the anxious soul is not toward self-management but toward covenantal deposit of the burden with the God who will not allow the righteous to be shaken.

Isaiah 41:10 (“fear not, for I am with you”) — the “fear not” commands of Isaiah's latter chapters (chs. 40–55) address exiled Israel with the same logic Jesus uses in Matthew 6: the covenant-keeping God's presence is the ground for releasing anxious preoccupation with earthly contingency.

Matthew 6:25–34 (Jesus' threefold prohibition) — the command “do not be anxious” appears three times, each time grounded in a different argument: creation care (6:26), the uselessness of worry (6:27), lily-clothing (6:28–30), the Gentile alternative (6:32), and the kingdom-first command (6:33).

Philippians 4:6–7 (prayer-peace link) — Paul's command is the New Testament's most direct application of the Jesus tradition on worry: the antidote is specific, thankful prayer; the result is the peace of God that guards the heart and mind; the mechanism is entrusting the burden to the sovereign God.
usage: Jesus' identification of worry as “what the Gentiles seek” (Matthew 6:32) is the sharpest pastoral rebuke: the Christian who worries is functionally living as if he had no covenant Father, as if prayer were ineffective, and as if the kingdom were not yet real — the pastoral call is not to calm the feelings but to renew the faith that generates peace.

The Philippians 4:6 command to bring every worry to God in specific, thankful prayer is not a psychological technique but a theological discipline: it is the act of faith that hands the burden back to the sovereign God and receives, not the resolution of the circumstance, but the peace that surpasses understanding.

Pastors who preach Matthew 6:25–34 must hold together the command (“do not be anxious” — this is a theological disorder) and the gospel ground (“your heavenly Father knows what you need” — this is a gospel promise): the command makes sense only as a call to renewed faith in the Father who governs all things for His children's good.
